Founding History
The Founding History of API Group traces back to 1926 when Rubin Anderson started a small
plumbing company in St. Paul, Minnesota.
Over time his company grew.
And a division focused on insulation contracting and distribution emerged, which would become
the roots of what we now know as API Group today.
In 1948, this division was incorporated as a separate company.
And a few decades later, in 1964, leadership transitioned to the next generation.
The family business continued to diversify, particularly into construction and construction
related industries.
Well, at the same time, starting to expand globally, 2002 marked their next phase when
current CEO and president of API Group, Russell Becker, took over after spending seven years
leading a subsidiary.
The most recent catalyst for the change came in 2019 when J2, a SPAC, acquired API Group
for 2.9 billion.
To understand API Group though, we have to know Martin Franklin.
Martin Franklin had a long history of acquiring companies through more traditional means, usually
buying underperforming companies that he felt had more potential to operationally improve
and a runway to acquire related businesses.
Martin Franklin's career began by partnering with his dad, a merchant banker, who was partners
with James Goldsmith, to LBO, a paper and packaging conglomerate.
He was just 24 at the time, and at the beginning of a long career of acquiring, improving,
and flipping companies.
Franklin's acquisitions have extended to various industries, including financial services,
media, fast food franchises, and consumer products.
The SPAC that acquired API Group, J2, was named after Jordan.
The original Jordan traces back to 2001, with an acquisition of Altrista, which was a spin
out from Ballcorp, which was renamed to Jordan at Deal Close.
In addition, focused on the consumer space, and acquired a variety of brands, including
Crockpot, Mr. Coffee, Coleman, and Yankee Candle, among many others.
Originally purchased for just $300 million in 2001, in 2015, they would sell Jordan
for $15 billion, making Martin Franklin an estimated $500 million in the process.
In 2017, Martin Franklin, alongside Jordan Business Partners James Lilly and Ian Ashkin,
led up J2 and raised $1.25 billion.
J2 was just the latest in a string of Franklin SPACs, dating back to 2006.
Other businesses he was involved in include restaurant brands international, which owns
thousands of Burger King's and Tim Hortons.
Elements solutions, a specialty chemicals producer, and nomad foods, a frozen foods conglomerate.
With the long history of deal-making and improving businesses, Martin Franklin's endeavors
into the safety and specialty services business through API Group in 2019 peaked the interest
of many investors who began to wonder how much the business could improve, and just how
long the growth runway could be.
In 2019, J2 acquired API Group for $2.9 billion, with the intention of improving their
existing operations and making it the vehicle for subsequent acquisitions in the commercial
safety solution space.
The purchase was funded in part by a $1.2 billion term loan.
At the time, API Group had around 4 billion in revenues and listed on the NYSE in April
of 2020.
In 2019, API Group had over 40 operating businesses with over 200 locations, primarily
all located in North America.
Their group of businesses served a variety of essential business needs like HVAC systems,
fire sprinklers, water and telecommunication infrastructure, electricity and natural gas
distribution systems, security systems, and fire alarms.
As James E. Lilly said in a 2019 press release quote, with the completion of this acquisition,
we began the next chapter for API Group.
Martin and I are excited to partner with the company's impressive leadership team in
the 15,000 leaders throughout the organization.
We look forward to building upon API's proven track record over organic growth, complemented
with Discipline M&A, to grow within its niche markets and capitalize on adjacent opportunities
to generate long-term value for stakeholders.
Immediately after acquisition, they started to face headwinds from COVID, which shut down
a lot of their business, revenues further contracted in 2020, because API Group deliberately
shifted focus to service revenues over contract revenues, which were lower margin and by
nature one time.
To grow service revenues, they focused on the inspection business, because for every dollar
they earned with inspection, they tend to generate an average of $3 to $4 of annual service
revenue.
This is because a business using API Group for inspections are more likely to continue
to use them for various maintenance services that might come up during and inspection.
Additionally, a lot of systems are statutorily required to be inspected and serviced regularly,
which is work they can take over.
The shift from contract services to higher margin service work had the byproduct of improving
revenue predictability and customer relations.
CEO Russell Becker in 2Q20 had this to say about the dynamic.
You see, people wake up one morning and they think to themselves, geez, we should be doing
more inspection and service work, and we should really get focused on that, and then they
try to move into the space.
The challenge for them is that they don't have the infrastructure development that we have,
and so this selling inspections first model for us, the intangible aspect of that, is the
ability to build better and stickier client relationships.
We have developed and grown an inspection sales force that sits inside all of our branch
offices across our business, and so for somebody to just walk off the street and say, hey,
I want to do your inspections, it's just not going to happen.
When you're dealing with reputable clients with the right end markets, it's about that
best value, and it's not about whether somebody can save them $220 on an inspection.
If you look at the segment of our business, the average project size is under 10 grand,
and that is because we're doing a gazillion inspections at $1,000 a pop.
And so even if somebody goes in and says, I can do it for 9.50, people don't care about
that $50, they care about the quality of work and making sure that it's done properly
and everything else.
And so when you have that infrastructure already built and in place and it's functioning,
it's very, very difficult for somebody to just walk in and take that work away from you.
So we feel good about the resiliency.
We actually have aggressive growth goals and are going to continue to move towards that.
Their original goal was to generate 50% of their revenue from services, which they would
meet a few years later.
To grow the service revenues had the added benefit of allowing them to be more selective
in contract revenue, so they can pick better higher margin projects.
As Russell Becker pointed out in the 2Q20 earnings call, they do not quote bid on projects,
because they are not competing primarily on price.
Many contracts may come to them through their inspection or services, where a client needs
to upgrade or build out their infrastructure.
In these instances, the client is more likely to use API group since they are ready
to trust them.
While the markets they operate in are very fragmented, API group is well positioned to consolidate
it, because small businesses are much more focused on winning large contracts, whereas
the API group system allows them to efficiently serve the smaller ticket size work that gets
less attention.
In 2021, at a city conference, CEO Russell Becker said, our business is highly fragmented.
The space in general is highly fragmented, and so for a small family on business saying
Minneapolis where we are, it's easier for them to go chase a $700,000 project, versus
chasing around $700,000 of revenue $10,000 at a time like our average project size.
Their initial goals were to grow EBITDA margins to 12% by 2023, versus 7% at the time.

engages directly with the seller, and similar to the reasons why someone may sell their
business to Constellation software.
Many of the owners look to sell to API group are concerned about finding the right steward
in home for their employees.

to a mid-single-digit multiple.
Low-chairman James Lilly should some light on their M&A philosophy, saying, quote,
I'm not going to die over $20 million price differential in something like SK Fire Safety
that really sets up a platform for us in Europe, and can help our existing businesses

As of 2021, they had over 200 locations, and were the number one provider of fire protection
in life safety services.
These are high-quality businesses because legally customer facilities are required to be
inspected, at least annually, and sometimes more.
This allows API group to not only drive recurring revenue with inspections, but the services
they provide help to keep their customers up to code.
The inspection and service revenues are sticky and keep them in contact with their customer,

API group cross-sell services like adding fire extinguisher inspections when they're ready

Chubb is a full-service provider of fire and electronic security services.
They design, install, service, and monitor security and fire systems.
In contrast to API group who was primarily based in North America, Chubb's presence was

With 13,000 Chubb employees, the transaction doubled API size.
The acquisition pushed API service mix to over 50% of total revenues, and so they raised

This is prized revenue because not only are service revenues usually recurring, but inspections

In 2022, they had an investor day which showed their progress on long-term targets.
Whereas revenues were just 1.7 billion in 2012, they reached 6.5 billion, only 10 years

Over the next few years, API group would continue to focus on high-quality revenue sources,
